accepted.question_text: For a general control system Σ = (M, U, F) on a manifold M and a closed target set A ⊆ M, what sufficient conditions guarantee the existence of feedback laws that locally asymptotically stabilize A? In particular, when can one certify that A can be rendered invariant, that there exists a dynamical system for which A is at least a local attractor, and that these sufficient conditions are constructive enough to lead to actual controller design rather than only existence statements? A further part of the problem is to identify appropriate canonical classes of control systems in which such constructive sufficient conditions might be formulated.

evidence.quote: Sufficient conditions: Controllability assumptions, the existence of a control-Lyapunov functions or structural properties like homogeneity can be exploited to provide sufficient conditions for certain feedback laws to exist. It would be interesting to see to what extent these results can be generalized to work for general control systems, e.g., Σ =(M,U,F), aiming at locally asymptotically stabilizing some closed set A⊂M.
Hence, sufficient conditions, especially conditions that lead to the construction of controllers are of great importance

accepted.question_text: Can one develop computationally tractable topological and numerical tools that decide, a priori, whether a given stabilization problem admits a solution, with checks that are easier than brute-force numerical experimentation and that still provide certificates of accuracy when the control law or vector field data are noisy, approximate, or experimentally obtained? Computational homology and topological data analysis are proposed as possible ingredients in such certified decision procedures.

evidence.quote: Numerical tools: This line of work aims to provide necessary and sufficient conditions so that one can assess—a priori—if a stabilization problem has a solution. Clearly, these conditions must be easier to check than a brute force numerical experiment for this to be of practical value.
computational tools must be able to provide certificates of accuracy

accepted.question_text: Which new topological invariants, short of a complete conjugacy classification, can still capture qualitative behavior relevant to stability and stabilization of dynamical and control systems on manifolds? In particular, can one choose the homotopy appearing in the cited asymptotic-stabilization obstruction result so that the entire homotopy is itself asymptotically stabilizing, and can an analogous invariant-based program be extended beyond autonomous dynamical systems to general input-output systems in a compositional way?

evidence.quote: Other invariants: Although finding the “perfect” invariant that allows for classifying dynamical systems up to conjugacy (Smale program) is too ambitious, one might look for new invariants that capture (some) qualitative behaviour of interest.
can the homotopy from Theorem 6.13 be chosen to be asymptotically stabilizing throughout?
it is not clear how to meaningfully extend this type of theory to generic input-output systems. In other words, can a similar program be outlined for general systems

accepted.question_text: How can one identify a nonlinear system, or at least an appropriate global equivalence class of nonlinear systems, from data at a global scale rather than only along finite trajectories or in local neighborhoods? In particular, how can one detect unstable equilibria and build a theory combining topological methods, topological data analysis, and modern high-dimensional probability, while also clarifying how approaches such as neural networks, Gaussian processes, and Koopman-operator methods can be developed into a global identification framework?

evidence.quote: Nonlinear system identification: Our understanding of statistical finite-trajectory nonlinear system identification is improving, yet it is unclear how to go about identifying a nonlinear system (or equivalence class) globally. In particular, unstable equilibria are hard to identify.
Combining the topological viewpoint with TDA and modern high-dimensional probability theory ... could be a fruitful combination.

accepted.question_text: How can one formulate a principled theory of topological obstructions to stabilization that is invariant under feedback reparametrization rather than depending on a particular parametrization of the control system? More concretely, the open problem is to replace obstruction results that rely on a chosen control-system presentation with feedback-invariant statements depending only on genuinely intrinsic data, such as the underlying manifold M and the target set to be stabilized, while still retaining useful system-specific conclusions when necessary.

evidence.quote: Feedback invariance: As set forth in the monograph by Lewis, the lack of feedback-invariance present in most of the literature obstructs a principled control theory.
a variety of results, mostly contained in Sect. 6.1.1 do rely on the control system parametrization

accepted.question_text: What is the most meaningful way to extend obstruction-theoretic stability and stabilization results from deterministic systems on manifolds to stochastic systems with disturbances? Existing noise-aware results often focus on moments, but the open problem is to build a genuinely satisfactory stochastic analogue of the deterministic topological theory.

evidence.quote: Stochastic systems: One can generalize Definition 5.5 to include disturbances ... however, how to extend the theory in the most meaningful way to stochastic systems is not clear.

accepted.question_text: What additional theory and invariants can handle stabilization problems in which the relevant attractor or target set has Euler characteristic zero, a regime that includes many abundant examples such as odd-dimensional manifolds, Lie groups, and periodic orbits? These cases are especially difficult, so the problem is to develop methods that improve on the current reliance on retraction theory or otherwise yield a finer classification of zero-Euler-characteristic situations.

evidence.quote: Zero Euler characteristic: Set with zero Euler characteristic are inherently difficult to handle
As these sets are, however, abundant (odd-dimensional manifolds, Lie groups, periodic orbits), more theory is needed.
